title: Area of Circles and Sectors

findings.finding: The diameter example substitutes radius 7 cm without stating how it follows from the labelled diameter 14 cm.
findings.breakdown: The conversion from the given diameter to the radius is an essential decision, but its connecting calculation is absent from the worked example.
findings.checked: p3-radius-diameter rehearses halving, and p4-key-ideas-3 later states the rule. Neither supplies the connecting line in this example. The diagram labels only the diameter; its marks do not directly supply 7 cm.
findings.assumptions: Calculator availability does not affect this decision.

repair.proposal: Before substitution, add: 'The diameter is 14 cm, so r = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm.'

findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly connects the labelled diameter to the radius used in the formula.

findings.finding: The major-sector example substitutes 290° without stating how it follows from the labelled exterior angle 70°.
findings.breakdown: Selecting and calculating the interior angle is essential to the method, but the worked example omits that connecting step.
findings.checked: p10-identify teaches the interior/exterior relationship and practises it. Nevertheless, p11-sector-example-right labels only 70° and substitutes 290° without a calculation or sentence connecting them.
findings.assumptions: Calculator availability does not affect angle selection.

repair.proposal: Before substitution, add: 'The 70° angle is outside the sector, so θ = 360° − 70° = 290°.'

findings.doneWhen: The worked example explicitly derives the interior angle used in its area calculation.

findings.finding: One comparison with fixed radius would expose how sector area varies with interior angle; the two proposed runs serve the same purpose.
findings.breakdown: The supplied sector examples and guided practice change radius as well as angle. A single earlier run would also prepare students for the mixed practice.
findings.checked: For radius 6 cm, angles 30°, 60°, 120° and 240° give areas 3π, 6π, 12π and 24π cm². The follow-up gives 10π cm². These require only the sector formula already taught. p28-q8 later isolates angle, but comes after both proposed placements.
findings.assumptions: Radii are positive and angles are interior angles measured in degrees.

repair.proposal: After p11-sector-guided, add one optional run: 'Each sector has radius 6 cm. Predict how the areas compare before calculating. Find the exact areas for interior angles 30°, 60°, 120° and 240°. Explain what changes and what stays fixed.' Expected areas: 3π, 6π, 12π and 24π cm²; area doubles when the angle doubles at fixed radius. Follow with: 'Find the exact area of a sector with radius 5 cm and interior angle 144°.' Expected answer: 10π cm². Do not repeat the run after p15-q1.

findings.doneWhen: One run isolates the effect of angle, includes prediction and explanation, and ends with an unpatterned question.

findings.finding: Generalise the cancellation in the paired composite figures.
findings.breakdown: The task extends the existing request to add the two areas by asking students to explain why the semicircle contributions cancel.
findings.checked: Adding R + πr²/2 and R − πr²/2 gives 2R. With radii a and b, the sum is 2R + π(a² − b²)/2, equal to 2R exactly when the nonnegative radii are equal. Only previously used area formulas and algebra are needed.
findings.assumptions: Each removed semicircle fits inside its rectangle; radii are nonnegative.

repair.proposal: After p20-q4-total, add an optional task: 'Two identical rectangles each have area R. A semicircle of radius r is attached to one, and an equal semicircle is removed from the other. Predict their combined area and explain without evaluating π. What happens if the attached and removed semicircles have different radii a and b?' Expected answer: 2R for equal radii; otherwise 2R + ½π(a² − b²), which equals 2R only when a = b.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the cancellation and identify the condition under which it holds.

findings.finding: Generalise the relationship between sector area and radius at a fixed angle.
findings.breakdown: Students can use the sector formula and inverse operations to explain radius scaling without selecting numerical radii.
findings.checked: At the same positive angle, an area ratio of nine gives a squared-radius ratio of nine and a radius ratio of three. p28-q8-g and p28-q8-h already compare fixed-angle sectors with doubled radius. The optional arc-length component would depend on the unresolved prior teaching addressed by the merged context question, so it is omitted.
findings.assumptions: Both radii and the common sector angle are positive.

repair.proposal: After p30-q12, add an optional task: 'Two sectors have the same central angle. The second has nine times the area of the first. Without choosing numerical radii, explain how their radii compare. Does your conclusion still follow if their angles differ?' Expected answer: the second radius is three times the first, because the common angle factor cancels and r₂² = 9r₁². With different angles, the area ratio alone does not determine the radius ratio.

findings.doneWhen: Students derive the radius ratio and explain why fixing the angle matters.

findings.finding: Generalise the shaded fraction when the ratio of concentric radii changes.
findings.breakdown: The task retains the existing half-ring structure and asks students to explain how the radius ratio controls the shaded fraction.
findings.checked: With inner radius r > 0 and outer radius kr, k > 1, half the ring divided by the outer-circle area is (k² − 1)/(2k²). This is less than one half for every finite k > 1; k = 2 gives 3/8. Circle area, subtraction and fractions suffice.

repair.proposal: After p34-q11, add an optional task: 'The inner radius is r > 0 and the outer radius is kr, where k > 1. Half the ring is shaded. Find the shaded fraction of the outer circle. Can it ever equal one half? Explain.' Expected answer: (k² − 1)/(2k²), always less than one half because the inner circle has positive area; k = 2 gives 3/8.

findings.doneWhen: Students derive the fraction and explain why it cannot equal one half.

contextQuestions.question: Before this booklet, have students learned to calculate sector arcs as fractions of circumference and to find perimeter by adding the exposed straight edges? Length v1 may supply this, but its contents are not given. p28-q8-a supplies a half-circumference example without stating the general method. The answer determines whether the later arc-length and perimeter tasks need a short teaching addition.

dropped.reason: The mathematics is correct for positive diameters, but this exceeds the four-suggestion limit. The retained radius-scaling and concentric-circle extensions develop the same squared-size relationship more directly within their topics.

This suggestion is a weaker fit at the end of sectors than the retained fixed-radius variation, and is excluded under the four-suggestion limit.
